Q: Is there any substitute for SSH A:

The ssh flag -C can be used to ask for compression from the SSH server, which in some cases may make your connection faster, but is unlikely to be helpful in this case because of what you mentioned about the ping time.

Another flag you might find helpful is the -c flag which allows you to request a specific cipher to use from the server, I've heard good things about blowfish for this sort of problem.

To use both of these commands when SSHing you can try this:

ssh -C -c blowfish-cbc username@server

Finally, there are certain protocols like telnet or rsh (which are considered by many to be obsolete for this purpose) that do not use encryption, which may make your connection faster, at the cost of it being less secure.

Q: ABS(-2147483648) remains negative A:

To illustrate it in a more graphical way, in pure mathematical notation (nothing to do with computers or computer languages,) 2,147,483,64810 equals 100000000000000000000000000000002 — That is, a "one" followed by 31 "zeroes." But if you pack those same thirty-two binary digits into the bits of a 32-bit, signed integer variable in most computer languages, that's how the number -2,147,483,64810 is represented.

As others here have already said, there is no 32-bit signed integer value that represents positive 2,147,483,64810. When the true mathematical result of an operation such as ABS does not "fit" in the data type, we call that an overflow, and different computer languages have different ways of dealing with it. In some systems an overflow will cause something like an "exception" or a "signal" that is hard for your program to ignore. In some systems there will be an error code you can check if you want to. And, in still other systems, you just get a bogus result.
